Deep inside the Tibesti mountains of northern Chad, in the central Sahara, the town of Miski sits surrounded by a succession of never-ending wadis.
A couple of families live at the top of each of these valleys and in August, when the rainy season comes, the wadis become a river that washes through the mountains. When the rains go, the valleys become green and camels feed on them.
A remote volcanic range characterised by rugged, bare rock, rivers of lava and volcanoes that climb to 3,000 metres, the Tibesti, which runs through northern Chad across the border into southern Libya, is sometimes called the roof of the Sahara.
These mountains are home to the Tubu, an indigenous community whose territory also includes a part of southern Libya, northern Niger and northwestern Sudan.
And the valleys that surround the town of Miski contain vast deposits of a precious metal that throughout human history has been prized almost above anything else: gold.
The mountains, too, are filled with antimony, a toxic heavy metal that is putting the ecosystem of this indigenous community at severe risk and is also exported in great quantities.
For decades, the gold that sits in this remote place has been one of the drivers of armed conflict between the Tubu and the Libyan then Chadian states.

In 2021, Israeli police arrested a Palestinian man known as R, who after multiple rounds of torture, signed a confession document for a crime he did not commit.
He is one of hundreds of Palestinians featured in a report by the Public Committee Against Torture in Israel (PCATI) who faced criminal proceedings on the basis of confessions extracted under duress.
The man, whose name was withheld for fear of reprisals, spent months in prison before video footage showed he had been nowhere near the scene of the crime he was accused of.
Before that video came to light, R repeatedly tried to withdraw his confession to the unspecified crime but was tortured by Shin Bet officials regardless.
He and his brother, who had also faced charges, eventually secured acquittals and their release.
Theirs was a rare case of acquittal within an Israeli justice system where torture, sexual assault, rape and inhuman treatment have become normalised, according to multiple reports from human rights organisations and the UN.
In its report, PCATI profiled 42 cases it had filed over the past decade on behalf of Palestinians who reported torture during Shin Bet interrogations.
In 33 of those cases, Palestinian detainees confessed under torture during or after questioning.
Israeli courts only recognised four of those confessions as false, despite interrogators using torture on the detainees.
The report describes how a confession extracted under duress can make its way into a criminal case.

Rahma Hegy, Fosis vice-president for student affairs, said Muslim students continued to make significant contributions to university life and wider British society, despite feeling unwelcome on campus.
"Many [students] tell us they do not feel they belong on the very campuses meant to include them," Hegy told Middle East Eye.
"They face discrimination, and too often they stay quiet because they do not expect anyone to be held accountable."
Hegy said the lack of accountability was among the organisation's greatest concerns and urged universities, student unions and the government to act on it.
The findings are based on responses from 715 students across 63 higher education institutions in the UK, making it one of the largest recent surveys of Muslim students' experiences at British universities.

The president of the world's highest court, Yuji Iwasawa, concluded that Myanmar had the "intention to destroy" a substantial part of the Rohingya population and tried to hide its crimes through "extensive destruction of evidence".
During so-called "clearance operations" in 2017, Myanmar's security forces from the Buddhist-majority state of Myanmar killed at least 10,000 Rohingya, a Muslim minority, and drove more than 700,000 from their homes in northern Rakhine state. Most found refuge in Bangladesh.
Entire villages were erased, evidence destroyed by burning bodies and bulldozing sites, and the Rohingya subjected to campaigns of rape and sexual violence. Myanmar failed to prosecute the perpetrators.

The US Department of State has a 12-year backlog of alleged cases of gross human rights violations in Israel to adjudicate, because the agency has made little effort to trace the end point of US military assistance there, a report quietly posted online by the Office of the Inspector General (OIG) last month showed.
The findings "demonstrate that the Department has created an unlawful de facto exemption to the law for Israel", Charles Blaha, a state department official who retired in 2023, wrote in a piece for Just Security on Monday.
The OIG report hones in on the application of the Leahy Law, which prohibits US assistance to any foreign security forces unit if the secretary of state has credible information that such a unit has committed "gross violations of human rights".
In a September 2025 report to Congress, the state department said the only units it had assessed to be ineligible for US security assistance were in Ukraine, Egypt and Jordan - even though Israel had previously been cited as having non-traceable assistance (NTA).
The NTA means the state department "cannot identify recipient units in advance of the transfer of assistance or training, or the units are not known with sufficient detail to make Leahy vetting possible", the OIG report said.
It concluded that the state department "had not developed or distributed comprehensive guidance and training to help staff implement NTA vetting requirements", and that nearly half of all missions overseas "did not respond to annual requirements to certify if a country was receiving NTA".

A US federal judge on Monday permanently barred the Trump administration from punishing rights groups who liaise with the International Criminal Court (ICC).
The ruling extends to all Americans, and not just the plaintiffs in the case.
Judge Jesse Furman of the Southern District of New York first issued a temporary injunction last month.
This week he ruled that while "the Government effectively requests that the Court reconsider its earlier decisions ... there is no merit to that request".
"Put simply, Plaintiffs demonstrate that the Services Prohibition is a content-based restriction on speech and that it is not narrowly tailored to serve compelling state interests," Furman wrote.
Democracy for the Arab World Now (Dawn), founded by the late Middle East Eye columnist Jamal Khashoggi, filed the lawsuit in July.
In October, Furman blocked the Trump administration from potentially imposing civil or criminal liability on the group as well as another allied organisation, the Taxpayer Alliance Against Genocide (Taag), for any work carried out with the ICC.
"Anyone violating this prohibition could face up to 20 years in prison and up to $1 million in civil fines," Dawn said in a press release on Tuesday.
"Because the government can interpret the term 'services' to encompass anything that confers a benefit on the recipient, Americans before this ruling risked criminal prosecution for submitting evidence about possible crimes to the ICC, or for exchanging information with and engaging in joint advocacy with the Palestinian human rights groups and Special Rapporteur [Francesca] Albanese."

Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis have pushed as close as 60 km to Aden, the temporary capital of the country's internationally recognised government, but they will not capture the city, Yemen's military said on Tuesday.
"I'll speak to you frankly. The situation is not where we want it to be. But it's not as dire as reported," Colonel Majed Abdullah Al-Nuzaily, spokesperson for Yemen's armed forces, told a group of reporters via video link.
Since fighting resumed in Yemen in July in parallel with the wider Iran war, the Houthis have rapidly advanced in Yemen, seizing territory from the internationally recognised government and its allies, who are backed by Saudi Arabia.
The Saudis have carried out air strikes on Yemen in support of their allies on the ground, while the Houthis have struck Saudi oil targets, airports and office towers.
Aden, now the target of Houthi missile and drone strikes, had previously not seen major hostilities since street battles in 2015, soon after the internationally recognised government fled Houthi-run Sanaa and made the port city its base.

Eighty years after the International Court of Justice (ICJ) first sat in The Hague, I walked into the Peace Palace’s Great Hall of Justice to photograph the judges as they took their seats.
They were about to deliver a landmark judgment in a trailblazing case brought by The Gambia against Myanmar. For the first time, the court would find that a state had committed genocide, the "crime of all crimes" as it has been described.
It had been seven years since The Gambia, a slither of a country of less than three million people in West Africa that is named after the river that dissects it, filed the case.
It argued that Myanmar was trying to destroy the Rohingya, a predominantly Muslim minority that has lived in Rakhine State on the country's western coast for generations.
The case was brought under the 1948 Genocide Convention, the UN’s first human rights treaty, drawn up in the wake of the Holocaust to define genocide under international law and require states to prevent and punish it.
In the past, international criminal tribunals have convicted individuals of genocide, such as in courts created to prosecute atrocities committed during the wars in the former Yugoslavia and in Rwanda in the 1990s.

In 2017, Myanmar’s military burned Rohingya villages, carried out mass killings and widespread rape, and deliberately killed children, the court found. Soldiers shot civilians as they fled, including people trying to swim to safety.

“It is very bad that we have reached this point. It is a real earthquake,” said Eliav Lieblich, a professor at Tel Aviv University’s law faculty.

The ICJ on Thursday concluded in a 9-6 decision that Myanmar's security forces had committed genocide against the Rohingya population in northern Rakhine State during the military's 2017 operations.
The judgment, the first time the UN's highest court has found a state responsible for genocide, offers South Africa a significant legal precedent in its case accusing Israel of committing genocide against Palestinians in Gaza, particularly over how judges assess genocidal intent when a state claims its military actions are driven by security objectives.

The number of active Rafale fighter jets in the Indian Air Force has fallen to 32 from 35 in the latest edition of an international military aviation directory, which has stirred renewed scrutiny of India's May 2025 military confrontation with Pakistan.
The revised figures, which appear in the 2027 World Air Forces directory published by British aviation magazine FlightGlobal, have renewed questions about the extent of Indian losses during Operation Sindoor.
Following the 22 April 2025 Pahalgam attack in Indian-administered Kashmir, India launched the military campaign on 7 May and attacked several targets deep inside Pakistan.
In the largest jet engagements of the 21st century, over 114 fighter jets were mobilised and engaged across the border.
Some 72 Indian Air Force (IAF) aircraft and 42 Pakistan Air Force (PAF) aircraft engaged each other in a confrontation that lasted roughly 50 minutes, according to military briefings and defence analyses.
Pakistan claimed to have shot down six Indian military aircraft, including three Rafales, during the confrontation.
New Delhi disputed the scale of Islamabad's claims but did not publish a detailed account of its own aircraft losses.
During a military briefing on 11 May, Air Marshal Awadhesh Kumar Bharti acknowledged that India had suffered aircraft losses but declined to identify the number or types involved.
“We are in a combat scenario and losses are a part of combat,” Bharti said.

Israel will probably lose the genocide case brought by South Africa if the International Court of Justice (ICJ) applies the reasoning it used last week to find Myanmar responsible for genocide against the Rohingya, an Israeli international law scholar has said.
“It is very bad that we have reached this point. It is a real earthquake,” said Eliav Lieblich, a professor at Tel Aviv University’s law faculty.
“Before jumping to conspiracy theories about the court, Israel has mainly itself to blame,” he wrote in a series of posts in Hebrew on X. “Even if you disagree with the majority on every legal point, no reasonable country should come anywhere close to falling short of the standards it set. In many respects, Netanyahu’s government dug this hole itself.”
The ICJ on Thursday concluded in a 9-6 decision that Myanmar's security forces had committed genocide against the Rohingya population in northern Rakhine State during the military's 2017 operations.
The judgment, the first time the UN's highest court has found a state responsible for genocide, offers South Africa a significant legal precedent in its case accusing Israel of committing genocide against Palestinians in Gaza, particularly over how judges assess genocidal intent when a state claims its military actions are driven by security objectives.
To prove the genocide, the ICJ first had to prove that genocidal acts were committed, then that there was a “specific intent” by the Myanmar state to destroy the group.

Israeli military suicides reach 16-year high
A total of 23 serving Israeli military personnel have died by suicide since the beginning of this year, the highest number recorded in the army since 2010, Haaretz reported on Monday.
At least 17 former soldiers also died by suicide in the past year, shortly after being discharged from military service, bringing the total number of serving and former soldiers who took their own lives to 40.
Suicides are not confined to Israel's military. Haaretz noted that five police officers also died by suicide in 2026.
According to official Israeli military data cited by the report, 73 officers and soldiers have died by suicide since the Hamas-led attacks in southern Israel on 7 October.

Solomona’s arrest resulted in a massacre of unarmed protesters by the New Zealand military and police.

Samoans around the world grew more curious, and have carried the flag at Palestine demonstrations. But the response was not all positive.
“Christian Zionism has got quite a strong stranglehold on Samoans and other people of the Pacific,” Mulipola tells Middle East Eye in a video call interview.
A self-described atheist, Mulipola was accused of not being truly Samoan, just because he did not support Israel.

Opinion: Anti-Muslim racism is a global system used to normalise mass killing
Dr Amina Shareef, a researcher of anti-Muslim racism, says that the destruction unfolding in Gaza, Iran and Lebanon is part of a longer history of anti-Muslim racism that has made mass Muslim suffering and death politically permissible.
She says that Islamophobia is not simply a matter of prejudice or discrimination, but a global system of racial power that constructs Muslims and those identified as Muslim as security threats, allowing violence against them to be justified in the name of security.
Central to this system is the figure of the Muslim terrorist, which portrays Muslim political agency as inherently threatening. Shareef says that this logic extends beyond surveillance, detention and militarised borders to warfare, political abandonment and the destruction of the conditions necessary for life.
She identifies Palestine as a key site where contemporary security practices and technologies of control have been refined and reproduced elsewhere, a process she describes through the concept of the “Palestine boomerang”. Although conflicts in Iran, Lebanon, Kashmir, Syria, Yemen, Iraq and Afghanistan have distinct histories, she argues that they reveal a recurring pattern in which Muslim populations are portrayed as threats and their suffering becomes easier to justify.
Shareef concludes that confronting anti-Muslim racism is ultimately a struggle to protect life and human dignity. She calls for sustained resistance to systems that expose entire populations to premature death, arguing that the responsibility to seek justice remains even when the outcome is uncertain.

Netanyahu, Eisenkot parties end talks without deal on forming government
The parties of caretaker Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his rival Gadi Eisenkot concluded a new round of talks on Sunday without reaching an agreement on a possible coalition government, which would require concessions from both sides.
Delegations from Eisenkot’s Yashar party and Netanyahu’s Likud met for four hours at a hotel in Herzliya, near Tel Aviv, following a first round of discussions last Sunday.
“The latest round of coalition talks… has concluded. The two sides outlined their positions on a range of substantive issues and discussed them in detail,” the two parties said in a joint statement.
“A follow-up meeting will be held,” they added, without specifying a date or revealing any other details.
A former army chief of staff, Eisenkot has until 6 December to form a government, with the possibility of a 14‑day extension, after October elections failed to give either camp an absolute majority.
His 48-member bloc, which needs 61 lawmakers to reach a majority, remains divided over whether to build a coalition through an alliance with ultra‑Orthodox parties, a rapprochement with Arab parties, or a national unity government with Likud.
Netanyahu is pushing for a national unity government, which could see a rotation of the premiership between the two men.

Cop31 ends in failure as countries reject climate deal over fossil fuels
The United Nations climate summit in Turkey became the longest-ever UN climate conference on Sunday as negotiations over a final agreement descended into deadlock, with the European Union and several other countries formally rejecting the proposed text.
The talks in Antalya, known as Cop31, continued more than 44 hours beyond their scheduled Friday conclusion, surpassing the previous record set by Cop25 in Madrid in 2019.
The latest draft, presented by the Turkish and Australian presidencies in an attempt to bridge divisions between countries, failed to secure consensus over its omission of explicit references to fossil fuels and disagreements over climate finance.
At the closing plenary, Cop31 President Murat Kurum acknowledged that countries had failed to agree on the proposed document.
“We have done our utmost. Ultimately, we have not imposed this text on anyone, nor have we issued an ultimatum such as a ‘take it or leave it’ demand,” Kurum said.
